passage:
Week one: Urmila volunteered to organise the Class 10 charity sale. She made a list of jobs and handed them out. By Friday, nobody had done anything. She did most of it herself and snapped at Pranav in the corridor.

Week two: Pranav stopped her after class. "You didn't ask what we wanted to do. You just told us." Urmila was stung, but she listened. At the next meeting, she asked people to choose their jobs. Pranav picked posters; he was good at drawing.

Week four: The sale ran out of samosas by noon. Someone had counted wrong. The principal asked who was in charge. Urmila swallowed. "Me. I checked the numbers and missed it." Pranav stood beside her.

qa.q: What job did Pranav choose?
qa.a: He picked posters because he was good at drawing.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when Pranav said she just told people what to do?
qa.a: She was stung and a bit hurt, but chose to listen, showing she wanted the project to work more than she wanted to be right.

qa.q: What changed in Urmila's leadership, and why did it work?
qa.a: She let people choose their own jobs, which gave them ownership, and she took the blame openly when the samosa count failed.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Urmila after she took the blame?
qa.a: He probably respected her more, which is why he stood beside her, since she didn't point fingers at others.

grounding: It shows a teen leader learning over weeks to motivate peers and take responsibility for a failure.

passage: Samir, beta, you've been made sports captain, so let me tell you about your Reena Didi. When she was in Class 11, she was the head of the school's science club. The first year she wanted everything perfect, so she did all the work herself. The others got bored and stopped coming. She came home crying. "Nobody helps me," she said. I asked her, "Did you ask them? Or did you do it before they could?" She was quiet for a long time. Next term she gave each member a small experiment to run and only helped when asked. One experiment failed at the school exhibition, and she stood up and said, "That's my fault, I didn't check the wiring." That's the day they started trusting her.

qa.q: What was Reena Didi the head of in Class 11?
qa.a: She was the head of the school's science club.

qa.q: Why did Reena Didi come home crying the first year?
qa.a: She felt alone and frustrated because the others had stopped coming, and she believed nobody would help her.

qa.q: What could Samir learn from Reena Didi's second term?
qa.a: He could give teammates real responsibilities, support them only when asked, and own mistakes openly so they trust him.

qa.q: How might the club members have seen Reena when she took the blame?
qa.a: They likely saw her as fair and brave, someone who protects the team rather than blaming them, so they began trusting her.

grounding: An elder tells a younger relative how a teen leader learned to share work and take blame when something failed.

passage: The science fair was two days away, and the school's power had gone for a day because of a storm. Sharmila, team leader for Class 9's solar model, had to reorganise everything. Her friend Kavitha was supposed to finish the panel, but she had fever and was home. Sharmila gathered the other three members in the dim classroom with a torch. "Okay. We've lost a day and a person. What can we still do well?" They split the work: one on wiring, one on posters, one on the talk. Sharmila called Kavitha to check on her and to ask how she'd planned the angles. On the day, the model worked, but one poster was crooked. The judge asked who made it. Sharmila said, "We rushed it. That's on me."

qa.q: Why was Kavitha unable to finish the panel?
qa.a: She had fever and was at home.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling in the dim classroom?
qa.a: She was probably stressed and worried about the lost day and missing member, but she stayed calm to keep the team focused.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that helped the team under pressure?
qa.a: She asked what they could still do well, split tasks clearly, stayed in touch with Kavitha, and took responsibility for the crooked poster.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel about Sharmila's phone call?
qa.a: She may feel cared for and still included, even though she was sick and couldn't be there.

grounding: It shows a teen leader organising peers under time pressure and taking blame for a flaw.

passage: Maria, seventeen, had spent six weeks organising the school's first charity food stall at the Bandra street fair. She'd made the rota, talked the canteen uncle into lending a stove, and kept seven tired classmates going with voice notes and jokes. On the day, the batter ran out at four, right when the crowd arrived. Simran had placed the order with the supplier, and some of the team were already whispering her name. When the principal walked up and asked what happened, Simran's face went white. Maria stepped forward. 'I checked the order list and missed it. It's on me.' Afterwards, in the empty stall, she told the team, 'Next year we make a stock checklist. Together.' Simran squeezed her hand.

qa.q: What ran out at four o'clock?
qa.a: The batter ran out at four, just as the crowd arrived.

qa.q: What might Simran have been feeling when the principal walked up?
qa.a: She was probably scared and ashamed, since she had placed the order and people were whispering her name.

qa.q: What does Maria's response show about leading a team?
qa.a: A leader takes responsibility for failures, protects teammates from blame and turns the mistake into a shared fix.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see Maria after this?
qa.a: They'd likely trust her more and be willing to work with her again next year. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teen organising peers, motivating them and taking blame when things fail.

passage: 'Bhaiya, it's a disaster.' Vikas flung his bag on the sofa. Deepak looked up from his laptop. 'The inter-class cricket?' 'Half the teams didn't turn up. The schedule clashed with the maths test.' 'Who made the schedule?' Vikas paused. 'Me. But nobody told me about the test!' 'Did you ask?' Silence. 'No.' 'Hmm.' Deepak closed the laptop. 'So what now, captain?' 'Everyone's angry. Some are saying it's the sports teacher's fault.' 'Is it?' Vikas rubbed his face. 'No. It's mine.' 'Then say that. And then?' 'Then… I send a new schedule. Check with all class reps first. Maybe get two people to help.' 'Now you sound like a leader.' 'I'll draft the message tonight.'

qa.q: Why did half the teams not turn up?
qa.a: The schedule clashed with the maths test.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he said 'It's mine'?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and a bit embarrassed, but was accepting that the mistake was his responsibility.

qa.q: What did Vikas plan to do to fix the tournament?
qa.a: Own the mistake, check with all class reps and send a new schedule, with two helpers.

qa.q: How might the sports teacher feel if Vikas had let the blame fall on the teacher?
qa.a: The teacher would likely feel unfairly blamed and lose trust in Vikas as a student organiser.

grounding: Shows a teen organiser learning to take blame when his project fails and plan better.

passage: Last term I, Kavitha, volunteered to lead our group's stall for the science fair. Five of us, one water-filter model, three weeks. I made a chart of jobs, and when Santosh got bored cutting bottles, I sat and cut with him and let him choose the music. We were good. Then, on the morning of the fair, I insisted on moving the model myself, fast, without waiting for the trolley. The sand layer spilled across the corridor. Everyone looked at Santosh, because he had been carrying the other end. I heard myself tell Sir, "It was my call. I rushed it." My face burned. But we rebuilt a smaller version by eleven, and Santosh explained the filter to the judges better than I could have. I still remember how fast the others knelt to scoop the sand once I'd said it.

qa.q: How many people were in Kavitha's group?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when telling Sir 'It was my call'?
qa.a: Kavitha felt ashamed, with a burning face, but also determined not to let Santosh be blamed for a rushed decision.

qa.q: What worked in Kavitha's leading before the fair, and what could change next time?
qa.a: Sharing the boring work and letting Santosh pick the music kept the group going; next time Kavitha could wait for the trolley instead of rushing under pressure.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Kavitha after she owned the mistake?
qa.a: Santosh was about to be blamed, so he probably felt relieved and more loyal, which may be why he explained the filter so well to the judges.

grounding: A student leading a science fair group takes the blame for a spill she caused, and the team rallies.

passage: Advisor's note, school magazine, 3 March. Hafsa (Class 11) took over as student editor when the last one left mid-term. Nine days to print, four pages empty. She split the team by strength: Jeevan on photos, two juniors on interviews, herself on layout. When the juniors stalled, she didn't scold; she sat with them and wrote the first question together. Two days before print, the interview with the canteen staff vanished from the shared folder. Hafsa came to me first: "I moved the files and didn't tell anyone. That's on me." She then asked Jeevan to help redo it at lunch. The issue went out one day late but complete. I will suggest her for the junior leadership workshop and share the file-sharing lesson with the whole team. — Ms D'Souza, magazine advisor

qa.q: How many days were left before print when Hafsa took over?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been feeling when admitting the missing files to Ms D'Souza?
qa.a: Hafsa was probably anxious and embarrassed about the lost interview, yet responsible enough to name her own mistake before anyone else was blamed.

qa.q: How could Ms D'Souza support Hafsa's growth as a leader from here?
qa.a: Ms D'Souza could praise the honest ownership and help Hafsa set a simple rule for moving shared files, as the note already plans.

qa.q: What is it like for Jeevan to be asked to redo the interview at lunch?
qa.a: Jeevan loses a lunch break, but because Hafsa owned the mistake first, the request probably feels fair rather than like being blamed.

grounding: A teacher's note records a student editor organising the team, motivating juniors and owning a file mistake.

passage:
Saturday night
The colony cricket tournament was MY idea, so today was my fault too. I booked the ground, made the fixtures, got Amandeep's team to turn up by promising samosas at the break. Worked great till 2 pm. Then Mr Bhalla came out and said nobody had asked the society office, and we had to stop mid-match. Everyone groaned. Amandeep said, "You said it was sorted!" I wanted to say the office never replies anyway. Instead I said, "I skipped that step. Sorry, guys." Then I walked to the office with Amandeep's dad and we got Sunday afternoon approved, on paper. Felt sick the whole walk. Now I've messaged everyone the new time. Twelve thumbs up so far 👍 Maybe leading is mostly fixing.
— Kashish

qa.q: Why did the match have to stop at 2 pm?
qa.a: Nobody had asked the society office.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling on the walk to the office?
qa.a: Kashish felt sick with guilt and nervous about having let everyone down, but kept going to fix it rather than hide.

qa.q: What small step would have prevented the stoppage?
qa.a: Getting written permission from the society office before booking the ground, which is exactly what Kashish did afterwards for Sunday.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see the apology?
qa.a: Amandeep was annoyed and felt misled by 'it was sorted', but a plain apology plus an approved new time probably made the frustration easier to drop.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows organising a colony tournament, a failure from a skipped step, and owning it.

passage:
Ganga: ok so the cleanliness drive was a disaster 😩

Ganga: it rained, half the volunteers didn't come and we forgot gloves
Kashish: you did organise 30 people though
Ganga: and 12 turned up. that's on me. I didn't send reminders
Kashish: principal was fine about it
Ganga: I'm going to tell the group it was my fault, not the rain
Kashish: why??

Kashish: honestly that's why people follow you

Kashish: yes. Saturday?

What was Ganga feeling about the cleanliness drive?
qa.a: Ganga felt disappointed and frustrated with the drive and with Ganga's own planning.

qa.q: What does Ganga plan to do differently next time?

passage:
Yamini had convinced twenty teenagers in the village to start a small library in the old panchayat room. They collected two hundred books, painted shelves, and made a lending register.
On the opening day, the roof leaked in the rain. Forty books got soaked.
Everyone looked at Yamini. Ritu muttered, "Who checked the roof?"
Yamini's face burned. She could have blamed the panchayat. Instead she said, "I should have checked. That was my job."
Then she handed out tasks: Ritu and two others to dry books in the sun, others to move shelves, and herself to the sarpanch to ask for roof repair.
By evening, thirty books were saved. The sarpanch promised a new tin sheet.

qa.q: How many books got soaked?
qa.a: Forty books.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when her face burned?
qa.a: Yamini felt embarrassed and responsible for the leaking roof.

qa.q: What did Yamini do as a leader after the mistake?
qa.a: She took the blame, gave everyone clear tasks, and went to the sarpanch herself to fix the roof.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Yamini after the evening?
qa.a: Ritu probably respects her more, seeing that she owned the mistake and fixed it fast.

grounding: A village teen leading a library project takes responsibility when it goes wrong.

passage:
In Melbourne, Bao led the school robotics team. For three months they built a robot to sort recycling. At the regional competition, it froze on the first task.
The team stood around, silent. Nadia, who had written the code, looked like she might cry.
Bao spoke first. "I rushed the final test yesterday. I should've made us run it one more time. That's on me."
Nadia whispered, "But the code—"
"We check the code together next time. It's a team thing."
Then Bao gathered everyone. "What did we learn?" They listed four things on a napkin.
The judges gave them a prize for teamwork.

qa.q: How long did the team build the robot?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: What was Nadia feeling when she looked like she might cry?
qa.a: Nadia felt guilty and upset, thinking her code caused the failure.

qa.q: What did Bao do that made the team stronger?
qa.a: Bao took responsibility, protected Nadia from blame, and turned the failure into a list of lessons.

qa.q: What would change if Bao had blamed the code in front of everyone?
qa.a: Nadia would likely feel humiliated, the team might split into blaming each other, and they would learn less from the failure.

grounding: A teen robotics team leader in Australia takes blame after a failure and motivates the team.

passage:
Lalremsiami had volunteered to lead her class stall at the school science fair in Aizawl. She made a task chart: who builds, who explains, who brings materials. Raghav was supposed to bring the plywood base. He forgot. Twice.
She didn't shout. On Wednesday she asked him, "What's actually stopping you?" He admitted he didn't know where to get it. She paired him with Mr Lalthanga, the carpentry teacher, and Raghav came back proud, carrying the board himself.
On fair day, their water-filter model leaked all over the table in front of the principal. The group froze. Lalremsiami stepped forward. "That's my fault, Ma'am. I didn't test the joints after we moved it." Then she mopped it up, fixed the joint with tape and restarted the demo.
Later Raghav said, "You didn't have to say it was your fault." She shrugged. "I was in charge."

qa.q: What did Raghav forget to bring twice?
qa.a: He forgot the plywood base.

qa.q: What does Raghav's comment afterwards suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Raghav felt surprised and grateful that Lalremsiami took the blame instead of pointing at the group.

qa.q: Which of Lalremsiami's leadership choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Raghav what was stopping him, instead of scolding, solved the real problem; owning the leak kept the team calm.

qa.q: How might the principal see Lalremsiami after the leak?
qa.a: The principal would likely respect her for taking responsibility and fixing it calmly instead of making excuses.

grounding: Illustrates a teen leading a project, motivating a peer and taking the blame when something fails.

passage:
Hi Gargi,
I owe you and the team an apology. The Sunday book drive for the village library was my idea, I booked the community hall, and I told everyone 9 a.m. I didn't check that the hall was already booked for a wedding till noon. You all waited outside in the sun for three hours, and half of you left.
That's on me, not the hall people and not the team.
What I've learned: confirm bookings in writing, and have a backup place. I've spoken to the principal, and we can use the school's front verandah next Sunday.
Could you help me call the people who left? You're better at that than me. I'll send everyone a proper plan with times and jobs by Wednesday, and I'll check it with you first.
Thanks for staying on Sunday. It meant a lot.
Karthik

qa.q: Why did the team wait outside for three hours?
qa.a: Karthik didn't check that the hall was already booked for a wedding till noon.

qa.q: How does Karthik feel about what happened on Sunday?
qa.a: Karthik feels guilty and responsible for the team waiting in the sun, and grateful that Gargi stayed.

qa.q: What did Karthik do well as a leader after the mistake?
qa.a: Karthik took the blame, named the lesson learned, arranged a backup venue and asked Gargi for help with what Gargi is good at.

qa.q: How might the team members who left feel when Karthik's plan arrives?
qa.a: They may feel less annoyed and more willing to return, since Karthik owned the mistake and gave clear times and jobs.

grounding: Shows a teen organiser taking blame for a failed event and motivating the team to try again.

passage:
You asked for the school magazine how I lead the robotics team, Harish. Honestly, I learned the hard way.
In Class 10 I was team captain. I did everything myself because I didn't trust anyone. The others got bored and stopped coming. Our robot didn't even move at the regional round.
The mentor asked me, "Who else touched the robot?" Nobody. That hit me.
So this year, I gave everyone a part they owned: Mehul the wiring, Gaurav the code, me the design. We met twice a week, and I made sure every meeting started with each person showing one thing they'd done.
At the state round, the arm jammed. Gaurav wanted to blame the wiring. I said, "I designed that joint. My fault. Let's fix it." We came fourth.
It's Yash, by the way, in case you print this. Put the team's names too.

qa.q: Who handled the wiring in Yash's team this year?
qa.a: Mehul handled the wiring.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the mentor asked who else touched the robot?
qa.a: Yash felt shaken and ashamed, realising Yash had shut the team out.

qa.q: What changes made Yash a better leader, and why did they work?
qa.a: Giving each person a part to own and starting meetings with everyone showing progress kept people motivated and responsible.

qa.q: How might Gaurav have felt when Yash took the blame at the state round?
qa.a: Gaurav was probably relieved and calmer, and maybe a bit embarrassed at having wanted to blame someone.

grounding: Illustrates a teen learning to share leadership, motivate peers and take blame when a project fails.

passage: I'm Leela, and I sat two benches behind Neelam the whole term, so I saw most of it. When Sir asked who would run the science-fair stall, nobody moved, and Neelam put her hand up. She drew a chart on the back of a notebook: who builds the water-filter model, who writes the poster, who explains it to visitors. She messaged the group every evening, not bossy, just "Anyone stuck?" On the day, the filter leaked all over the table and the judges frowned. I expected her to blame the boy who had sealed the joints. Instead she said, "I told him to rush it. That's on me." Her voice shook a little, I think. Afterward she asked each of us what she should do differently next time. I don't know what she felt inside, but I'd work with her again.

qa.q: What did the group build for the science-fair stall?
qa.a: They built a water-filter model.

qa.q: What does Neelam's shaking voice suggest about how she felt when she took the blame?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous and embarrassed about the failure, yet determined to own it instead of blaming a teammate, though Leela admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: What could Neelam try next time to avoid a last-minute leak?
qa.a: She could plan a test run a day early, so the group has time to fix problems instead of rushing the joints.

qa.q: What is it like for the boy who sealed the joints when Neelam says it is on her?
qa.a: He is spared being shamed in front of the judges, so he probably feels relieved and may trust her more as a leader.

grounding: Shows a student taking charge of a group project, keeping peers going, and accepting the blame when it fails.
